strengths: Novel and well-motivated contribution: to the best of reviewer knowledge, RadarGen is the first probabilistic (diffusion-based) generative framework for automotive radar point clouds (including RCS and Doppler attributes) conditioned on multi-view camera imagery, addressing a real gap in generative simulation, which has focused almost exclusively on vision and LiDAR.

Technically sensible design: the BEV rasterized representation with Point Density, RCS, and Doppler maps is a clean way to adapt a pretrained image-latent diffusion backbone (SANA) to sparse, unordered radar data without modifying the frozen autoencoder; the IRL1/LASSO deconvolution recovery step is a principled inverse-problem solution that exploits knowledge of the forward blurring kernel, and is well validated against peak/random sampling alternatives (Fig. 6, Fig. 10).

Comprehensive evaluation protocol: the paper proposes a thoughtful suite of metrics (CD-Loc, CD-Full, IoU@1m, Density Similarity, Hit Rate, Distance-Attribute, and per-class MMD) with full formulations in the supplement, and reports them separately for the entire area and foreground objects — an appropriate treatment given no standard benchmark exists for this task.

Consistent quantitative and qualitative evidence: RadarGen outperforms a carefully matched baseline (adapted RGB2Point with comparable parameter count) across most metrics; ablations confirm each conditioning modality (semantic, appearance, velocity) contributes meaningfully; a direct multi-view conditioning variant is also compared to justify the BEV design.

Demonstrated practical relevance: downstream detection results (VoxelNeXt achieving NDS 0.30 on generated vs. ~0 on baseline data), and controllable scene editing via off-the-shelf image editors (object removal/insertion correctly updating occlusion patterns), show the output is usable by perception models and supports the claimed simulation/augmentation use case.

Honest limitations discussion: dependence on foundation models, degraded performance in low-light/occlusion scenarios, and the double-edged nature of hallucinating occluded regions are clearly acknowledged, with qualitative analysis provided (Fig. 12).
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to a single dataset (MAN TruckScenes, with only 49 evaluation clips after filtering out low-light scenes), and training on only annotated frames. This raises concerns about generalization to other radar configurations, sensor placements, and geographic conditions; the limitations section concedes this, but a second dataset would have substantially strengthened the claims.

The evaluation metrics are proposed by the authors themselves; while reasonable, they are validated only by consistency of use across methods rather than against any external standard, and some metrics (e.g., DA with fixed thresholds of 1m/8dBsm/2.5m/s) involve arbitrary choices that may favor one model family over another. The large reported variances (e.g., DA Recall 0.23±0.12) suggest high metric noise on the small evaluation set.

The baseline comparison is thin: the only quantitative competitor is an adaptation of RGB2Point, a deterministic model not designed for this task. No comparison to other conditional generation approaches (e.g., Song et al., Alkanat et al., Xiao et al. adapted to this setting) is provided, making it difficult to judge absolute progress in the field.

The downstream detection gap remains large (NDS 0.30 vs. 0.48 on real data), and the explanation ('detector tailoring') is dismissed as beyond scope; a closer analysis of the real-vs-synthetic distribution discrepancy would better substantiate the claim that RadarGen narrows the sim-to-real gap.

Inference cost is significant (~10.5s per frame, with 9s spent on BEV conditioning map creation from foundation models), which weakens the claim of being deployable 'at scale' in simulation pipelines; scaling behavior and amortization strategies are not discussed.

The method inherits compounded errors from three upstream foundation models (metric depth, segmentation, optical flow); no analysis of sensitivity to their individual errors is given beyond the zeroing-out ablations, which do not reflect realistic degradation.

No mention of code or data release, which limits reproducibility of a paper that also introduces a new benchmark protocol. Minor issues: Doppler range of ±120 m/s in normalization appears implausibly wide for automotive radar relative to the actual attribute distribution; the claim of 'first' should be tempered given concurrent works like Xiao et al. and Rangeldm, which the related work does discuss.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored problem: probabilistic generation of automotive radar point clouds (location, RCS, Doppler) from multi-view camera imagery, positioned well against physics-based simulators, raw-data-based generators, and deterministic image-to-point-cloud regressors. The claim of being the first probabilistic diffusion framework for this task appears credible given the related-work coverage.

The technical design is sensible and well-motivated: converting sparse, non-grid-aligned radar detections into dense image-like BEV maps (Gaussian-smoothed density map, Voronoi-based RCS/Doppler maps) makes them compatible with a pretrained image latent diffusion backbone (SANA) without modifying the autoencoder; the L1-regularized deconvolution (IRL1/FISTA) for sparse point recovery is a principled inverse-problem formulation rather than an ad hoc heuristic, and the σ/recovery-method ablation (Fig. 6) supports this choice.

Comprehensive evaluation protocol: the authors introduce a well-specified metric suite (CD, IoU@1m, Density Similarity, Hit Rate, DA metrics, MMD) with full formulations in the supplement, evaluate both Entire Area and per-class Foreground statistics, and include a downstream compatibility test with a detector trained on real data (VoxelNeXt), which is the right test for a data-generation paper.

Fair ablations, including a comparison against direct multi-view image conditioning that honestly reports where the MV variant is better (attribute MMD), plus transparent implementation details, seeds, and a candid limitations section (hallucination in camera-occluded regions, dependence on foundation models, low-light failure shown qualitatively in Fig. 12).
weaknesses: Evidence breadth is limited for the scale of the claims: evaluation uses a single dataset (MAN TruckScenes) with only 49 evaluation clips, night scenes filtered out of training, and evaluation restricted to the small subset of annotated frames (40 per clip). Generalization across sensors, radar configurations, and datasets — central to the paper's 'scalable direction for multimodal generative simulation' claim — is untested.

The ablation study is weakly discriminating: removing the semantic, velocity, or appearance maps changes most metrics only marginally (e.g., full RadarGen Doppler MMD 0.31 vs. 0.34–0.35 without velocity/appearance, largely within reported variance), and several foreground MMDs are actually better without a condition (e.g., MMD Car Loc. 0.037 full model vs. 0.025 for MV conditioning, 0.033 without velocity). The claim that 'all input channels are meaningfully fused' is thus only loosely supported by the numbers.

The main baseline (an adapted RGB2Point) is a weak comparator: it is a deterministic feedforward model not designed for this task, uses only frame t while RadarGen uses t and t+Δt, and it essentially collapses on the detection test (NDS ≈ 0), making the headline comparison uninformative about the state of the art. The most informative comparison (direct MV conditioning) is relegated to an ablation and shows the BEV design trades attribute-distribution fidelity for geometry and speed.

The real-data domain gap remains substantial: detector NDS drops from 0.48 on real radar to 0.30 on generated data (mAP 0.38 → 0.11, mAVE 1.88 → 4.04), indicating that velocity attributes in particular are not yet realistic enough for downstream use; the paper acknowledges this but defers analysis as 'beyond the scope.'

Practicality concerns are under-addressed: inference takes ~10.5s per frame, 9s of which is BEV conditioning creation from foundation models — this undercuts the 'deployable in large scale simulation settings' claim; additionally, elevation is discarded entirely (2D BEV), so generated point clouds cannot be used where 3D structure matters, and the loss on CD Full (Entire Area) relative to the baseline is only partially explained.

Self-defined evaluation metrics introduce circularity risk: with no external benchmark, several metrics (DA thresholds, Density Similarity, per-class MMD aggregation) are bespoke, and some choices (e.g., IoU@1m with a 1m matching radius at ±50m range) are coarse. Minor polish issues further reduce confidence (e.g., 'Quantitavie' in the Table 1 caption; duplicate symbol Mp with inconsistent ranges in supplement B.1).

strengths: Novel and underexplored problem: the paper presents, to the authors' plausible claim, the first probabilistic diffusion framework for generating automotive radar point clouds (location, RCS, Doppler) from multi-view camera imagery, addressing a real gap where generative simulation has focused on vision and LiDAR but not radar.

Thoughtful representation design: the BEV encoding of sparse radar data (Gaussian-blurred point density map, Voronoi-based RCS/Doppler maps) is a principled way to make sparse, non-grid radar data compatible with a pretrained image autoencoder, and the L1-regularized deconvolution recovery is a clean, well-justified inverse problem formulation rather than an ad-hoc thresholding heuristic.

Comprehensive evaluation protocol: since no standard benchmark exists, the authors propose a broad suite of metrics (geometric fidelity, attribute fidelity via a new Distance-Attribute metric, distributional similarity via MMD) with full formulations in the supplementary, which is a useful contribution for future work.

Experiments go beyond metric tables: compatibility with a real VoxelNeXt detector, ablations of every conditioning map, comparison of BEV vs. direct multi-view conditioning, ablation of the reconstruction kernel/recovery method, and qualitative scene-editing demonstrations (occlusion-consistent object removal/insertion) strengthen the empirical case.

Honest and specific limitations section (dependence on foundation models, low-light failures, hallucination in camera-invisible regions), supported by a qualitative failure-case analysis in the supplementary.
Good reproducibility support: detailed training hyperparameters, seeds, inference-time breakdown, solver hyperparameters, and baseline adaptation details are provided.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single dataset (MAN TruckScenes, with night scenes filtered out) and a small evaluation set (49 clips, and only the 40/200 annotated frames per clip). No cross-dataset validation (e.g., nuScenes), which weakens generalization claims for a method whose main selling point is scalable conditioning on existing visual datasets.

The baseline comparison is weak: the only quantitative baseline is a repurposed RGB2Point model, not a method designed for radar generation. Closest related works (Song et al. [69], Alkanat et al. [2], Xiao et al. [82]) are discussed but not compared, so the magnitude of improvement over the state of the art is hard to gauge.

Several ablation gains are marginal and within reported standard deviations (e.g., IoU@1m 0.31 for RadarGen vs. 0.31 without semantic/velocity maps; DA Precision 0.26 vs. 0.25), and RadarGen is sometimes outperformed by ablated or even MV-conditioned variants on individual foreground MMD metrics. The claim that all conditioning channels are 'meaningfully fused' is only weakly supported; the text overstates the significance of small differences.

The downstream detection result reveals a substantial sim-to-real gap (NDS 0.30 vs. 0.48 on real data, mAVE 4.04 vs. 1.88) that the authors acknowledge but defer analysis of; this limits the practical utility claim for perception training/augmentation at this stage.

Inference cost is high (~10.5 s per frame, with 9 s spent creating BEV conditioning maps), which sits uneasily with the framing of a 'scalable' simulation solution; throughput/scalability is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The RCS and Doppler attributes are recovered by nearest-point retrieval from Voronoi-based maps, which couples attribute accuracy entirely to spatial accuracy; the implications of this design for attribute realism (e.g., multipath or spatially offset ghost detections) are not analyzed.

Some methodological choices are only empirically justified (e.g., σ = 2 chosen on a mini-train set; Voronoi attribute maps) and the stochasticity claims are validated mainly qualitatively (Fig. 9) without a diversity/coverage metric.
